facts.statement: The holotype skeleton of Parksosaurus was discovered in 1922 by a University of Toronto expedition in Alberta, Canada.
facts.quote: A 1922 expedition of the University of Toronto to what was then known as the Edmonton Formation (now the Horseshoe Canyon Formation) of Alberta uncovered the skeleton of a small dinosaur.

facts.statement: Professor William A. Parks first described the species in 1926, initially naming it Thescelosaurus warreni.
facts.quote: ROM 804 was first described in 1926 by University of Toronto professor William A. Parks, where it was identified as a new species of hypsilophodontid.

facts.statement: Charles Mortram Sternberg established the genus Parksosaurus in 1937 to separate it from Thescelosaurus.
facts.quote: ROM 804 was maintained as a species of Thescelosaurus until 1937, when American palaeontologist Charles Mortram Sternberg identified a new species of Thescelosaurus, at which time he named the new genus Parksosaurus for T. warreni.

facts.statement: The fossil was found approximately 0.5 miles from the Red Deer River and 100 feet above the water level near Rumsey Ferry.
facts.quote: The specimen was found around 0.5 mi from the Red Deer River and 100 ft above the water level, directly sound of the road that led to Rumsey Ferry.

facts.statement: Parksosaurus lived around 70 million years ago during the early Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous.
facts.quote: It is one of the few described non-hadrosaurid ornithopods from the end of the Cretaceous in North America, existing around 70 million years ago.

facts.statement: Fossils of Parksosaurus date to approximately 69.5 million years ago from the base of Unit 4 of the Horseshoe Canyon Formation.
facts.quote: Parksosaurus is known from the base of Unit 4 of the Horseshoe Canyon Formation, which dates to about 69.5 million years ago.

facts.statement: The habitat of Parksosaurus was influenced by the encroaching Western Interior Seaway, a shallow sea covering mid-North America.
facts.quote: The Horseshoe Canyon Formation is interpreted as having a significant marine influence, due to an encroaching Western Interior Seaway, the shallow sea that covered the midsection of North America through much of the Cretaceous.

facts.statement: Parksosaurus was a small, bipedal, herbivorous dinosaur known from a partially articulated skeleton and partial skull.
facts.quote: It is based on most of a partially articulated skeleton and partial skull, showing it to have been a small, bipedal, herbivorous dinosaur.

facts.statement: Parksosaurus possessed thin, partly ossified cartilaginous plates along its ribs, similar to Thescelosaurus.
facts.quote: Like Thescelosaurus, it had thin, partly ossified cartilaginous (intercostal) plates along the ribs.

facts.statement: Parksosaurus was likely a small, swift bipedal herbivore in life.
facts.quote: In life, Parksosaurus, as a hypsilophodont, would have been a small, swift bipedal herbivore.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that Parksosaurus had long toes adapted for walking on mud near rivers and strong forelimbs used for burrowing.
facts.quote: Paul in 2010 suggested that the long toes were an adaptation for walking over mud or clay near rivers and that the strong arms were used for burrowing.

facts.statement: Parksosaurus is classified within the family Thescelosauridae.
facts.quote: familia: Thescelosauridae

facts.statement: The species belongs to the subfamily Thescelosaurinae.
facts.quote: subfamilia: Thescelosaurinae

facts.statement: There is debate regarding the exact placement of Parksosaurus, with some studies suggesting it is the sister taxon to Thescelosaurus while others suggest it may be close to the South American genus Gasparinisaura.
facts.quote: Recent reviews have dealt with it with little comment, although David B. Norman and colleagues (2004), in the framework of a paraphyletic Hypsilophodontidae, found it to be the sister taxon to Thescelosaurus, and Richard Butler and colleagues (2008) found that it may be close to the South American genus Gasparinisaura.
